answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and traceable to the page. The Rev. Anthony Anderson says it to his wife Judith in Act II of The Devil’s Disciple, written in 1897 and first printed in Three Plays for Puritans (London: Grant Richards, 1901), p. 33 — where the wording matches the popular version almost exactly. The one thing quoters lose is that it is a character’s line, delivered with a smile, not a pronouncement in Shaw’s own voice.

source.heading: Act II — a minister teasing his wife

docMeta.dd: Three Plays for Puritans (London: Grant Richards, 1901), p. 33
The Rev. Anthony Anderson, to his wife Judith

source.excerpt:
JUDITH. Oh, I know it’s wrong to hate anybody; but—
ANDERSON [going over to her with humorous tenderness] Come, dear, youre not so wicked as you think. The worst sin towards our fellow creatures is not to hate them, but to be indifferent to them: thats the essence of inhumanity. After all, my dear, if you watch people carefully, youll be surprised to find how like hate is to love.
trail: 1897 — Shaw writes The Devil’s Disciple. The sentence belongs to the Rev. Anthony Anderson in Act II; Quote Investigator ↗ credits Shaw for the words he wrote in that play, while noting they are a character’s and may not reflect his own viewpoint.
1901 — First publication, in Three Plays for Puritans (London: Grant Richards). The line stands on p. 33 of the scanned first edition ↗, in the wording still quoted today.

1909 onward — The sentence leaves the stage. Quote Investigator ↗ records it in The G.B.S. Calendar in 1909 and in Rudolf Flesch’s Book of Unusual Quotations in 1957 — each time ascribed to Shaw, with Anderson and Judith left behind.
Today — The play text is freely readable: Project Gutenberg ↗ carries The Devil’s Disciple, written 1897, as public domain in the United States.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the scanned 1901 Grant Richards first edition, p. 33, which prints Shaw’s apostrophe-free contractions — “youre,” “thats,” “youll.” The Project Gutenberg text ↗ normalises them to “you’re” and “that’s,” which is the form that circulates today.

author.name: George Bernard Shaw
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Born in Dublin in 1856 and dead in Hertfordshire in 1950, Shaw wrote some sixty plays and spent five decades as the most quotable arguer in the English-speaking world — which is precisely why so many sentences he never wrote end up with his name attached. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925 and became the first person to add an Academy Award to it, for the screenplay of the 1938 Pygmalion. The Devil’s Disciple (1897) was the biggest success of his first decade in the theatre, an American Revolution melodrama he wrote partly to prove he could beat the melodramatists at their own game.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong anyway
misattribution.intro: Nobody stole this one — Shaw really wrote it. The distortions are subtler: a line of dialogue is promoted to doctrine, a preposition quietly loses a letter, and a different saying about indifference keeps getting filed alongside it.

items.who: Shaw, speaking in his own voice
items.why: It is dialogue. The Rev. Anthony Anderson says it to his wife Judith, who has just admitted she hates Richard Dudgeon, and the Act II text ↗ stages the delivery as “humorous tenderness.” Quote Investigator ↗ raises the same caution in its conclusion: the words were spoken by a character, and so may not reflect Shaw’s viewpoint.

Shaw wrote towards. The Americanised form without the -s is common in quotation databases — The Quotations Page ↗ prints “The worst sin toward our fellow creatures…” while citing the same Act II source.

“The opposite of love is not hate, but indifference” is a separate saying, routinely pinned on Wiesel. Quote Investigator ↗ credits Wilhelm Stekel’s 1921 The Beloved Ego for it and notes Wiesel used the expression in 1986. Shaw’s line makes a different claim — indifference is worse than hate, not love’s opposite.

misattribution.truthLine: Shaw wrote it in 1897, and it is there in black and white in the first edition: Three Plays for Puritans (1901), p. 33 ↗. Just remember a country minister is saying it to his wife, and enjoying himself.

context.heading: What Anderson is actually doing
lead: Judith Anderson has just confessed that she hates Richard Dudgeon — the local blasphemer her husband has cheerfully invited into their house. Her husband, the town minister, does not scold her. The stage direction has him cross the room “with humorous tenderness,” tell her she is not so wicked as she thinks, and hand her the line as a consolation: hating a man at least means you have noticed him.

The consolation is a trap. Anderson goes straight on to argue that married couples torment and police each other while treating their enemies with scrupulous courtesy — so Judith, he says, is probably fonder of Dudgeon than she is of him. She is “strangely touched — even appalled.” The rest of the play spends two acts collecting on that joke. Quoted alone, the moral survives intact; the mischief underneath it does not.
detailsBody: The phrase gets read today as a line about animals, but in the play it means the neighbours. Anderson is answering one woman’s complaint about one man, and the speech around it is entirely about husbands, wives and enemies in a New Hampshire town during the American Revolution. The sentence travels well into other arguments — it just did not start in one.
